title: Ἄνθρωπος λέοντα χρυσοῦν εὑρών
titleEn: The Man Who Found a Golden Lion
part: The Man Who Found a Golden Lion (Chambry 62 · Perry 71)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 62 (= Perry 71). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Δειλὸς φιλάργυρος λέοντα χρυσοῦν εὑρὼν ἔλεγεν· « Οὐκ οἶδα τίς γενήσομαι ἐν τοῖς παροῦσιν· ἐγὼ ἐκβέβλημαι τῶν φρενῶν καὶ τί πράττειν οὐκ ἔχω· μερίζει με φιλοχρηματία καὶ τῆς φύσεως ἡ δειλία.
sentences.tr: Deilos philargyros leonta chrysoun heurōn elegen· « Ouk oida tis genēsomai en tois parousin· egō ekbeblēmai tōn phrenōn kai ti prattein ouk echō· merizei me philochrēmatia kai tēs physeōs hē deilia.
sentences.l: A cowardly miser, having found a golden lion, kept saying: « I do not know what I shall become in the present circumstances; I have been thrown out of my wits and I have not what to do; love of money divides me, and the cowardice of my nature.
sentences.i: A cowardly miser found a golden lion and said: « I do not know what is to become of me in this pass. I am out of my mind and at a loss what to do: love of money pulls me one way and my native cowardice the other.
sentences.n: The whole fable is the miser's monologue; only the first four words are narration. ἐκβέβλημαι τῶν φρενῶν is a perfect passive, 'I stand thrown out of my senses'. τί πράττειν οὐκ ἔχω: ἔχω with an indirect question and an infinitive, 'I have no idea what to do'. μερίζει is singular before a pair of subjects — Greek regularly lets the verb agree with the nearer one.

sentences.t: Ποία γὰρ τύχη ἢ ποῖος δαίμων εἰργάσατο χρυσοῦν λέοντα ;
sentences.tr: Poia gar tychē ē poios daimōn eirgasato chrysoun leonta ;
sentences.l: For what fortune or what divinity wrought a golden lion?
sentences.n: δαίμων is not a demon but any unnamed divine power, the anonymous agency behind a piece of luck. Chambry prints the Greek question mark ; with a space before it, French printing-house style.

sentences.t: Ἡ μὲν γὰρ ἐμὴ ψυχὴ πρὸς τὰ παρόντα ἑαυτῇ πολεμεῖ· ἀγαπᾷ μὲν τὸν χρυσόν, δέδοικε δὲ τοῦ χρυσοῦ τὴν ἐργασίαν· ἅπτεσθαι μὲν ἐλαύνει ὁ πόθος, ἀπέχεσθαι δὲ ὁ τρόπος.
sentences.tr: Hē men gar emē psychē pros ta paronta heautēi polemei· agapāi men ton chryson, dedoike de tou chrysou tēn ergasian· haptesthai men elaunei ho pothos, apechesthai de ho tropos.
sentences.l: For my own soul, in the face of the present circumstances, wars with itself: it loves the gold, but it fears the workmanship of the gold; longing drives me to lay hold, but my character to keep off.
sentences.i: For my soul, faced with this, is at war with itself: it loves the gold, but dreads the shape the gold has been worked into. Longing drives me to lay hold of it; my nature drives me to keep clear.
sentences.n: τοῦ χρυσοῦ τὴν ἐργασίαν, 'the working of the gold' — that is, the fact that it has been made into a lion. That is the whole joke: he wants the metal and is frightened of the shape. In the last clause ἐλαύνει has to be supplied again with ὁ τρόπος, and the two infinitives depend on it.

sentences.t: Ὢ τύχης διδούσης καὶ μὴ λαμβάνεσθαι συγχωρούσης· ὢ θησαυρὸς ἡδονὴν οὐκ ἔχων· ὢ χάρις δαίμονος ἄχαρις γενομένη.
sentences.tr: Ō tychēs didousēs kai mē lambanesthai synchōrousēs· ō thēsauros hēdonēn ouk echōn· ō charis daimonos acharis genomenē.
sentences.l: O fortune that gives and does not allow [the gift] to be taken! O treasure having no pleasure! O favour of a god that has turned out graceless!
sentences.i: O fortune, that gives and will not suffer the gift to be taken! O treasure with no joy in it! O gift of heaven turned thankless!
sentences.n: Three exclamations in a row: the first with the genitive (the exclamatory genitive after ὤ), the next two with the nominative. χάρις … ἄχαρις is a deliberate jingle — a grace that is graceless — which English can only echo at a distance.

sentences.l: What manner am I to employ?
sentences.i: What course am I to take?
sentences.n: χρήσωμαι is a deliberative subjunctive — the mood of a man asking himself what he is to do. χράομαι takes the dative of the thing used.

sentences.l: To what contrivance am I to come?
sentences.i: What device shall I fall back on?

sentences.t: ἄπειμι τοὺς οἰκέτας δεῦρο κομίσων λαβεῖν ὀφείλοντας τῇ πολυπληθεῖ συμμαχίᾳ, κἀγὼ πόρρω ἔσομαι θεατής. »
sentences.tr: apeimi tous oiketas deuro komisōn labein opheilontas tēi polyplēthei symmachiāi, kagō porrō esomai theatēs. »
sentences.l: I shall go off to fetch the household slaves here, who must do the taking with their numerous joint force, and I myself shall be a spectator far off. »
sentences.i: I will go and bring my household slaves here to do the taking, a whole crowd of them at once, and I shall stand well off and watch. »
sentences.n: κομίσων is a future participle of purpose after a verb of going — the standard Greek 'in order to fetch'. κἀγώ is καὶ ἐγώ run together by crasis. The miser's solution is to have others touch the thing while he watches from a safe distance.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος ἁρμόζει πρός τινα πλούσιον μὴ τολμῶντα προσψαῦσαι καὶ χρήσασθαι τῷ πλούτῳ.
sentences.tr: Ho logos harmozei pros tina plousion mē tolmōnta prospsausai kai chrēsasthai tōi ploutōi.
sentences.l: The story fits a certain rich man who does not dare to touch and to use his wealth.
sentences.i: The story fits a rich man who dares neither touch his wealth nor use it.
sentences.n: A closing formula of its own kind: ὁ λόγος ἁρμόζει πρός…, 'the story fits…', close cousin of the commoner ὁ λόγος εὔκαιρος πρός…. Both aim the fable at a type of person rather than stating a maxim.
